- **OIG's own dashboard says 586 open, not 567.** The 19 extra are blank rows on OIG's pages. A row-by-row comparison found the same recommendations in both sets, so the gap is within tolerance and doesn't mean any recommendations are missing. Source: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/data-dashboard

| Year published | Open recommendations | Reports |

- For comparison, the full dataset has 15,649 recommendations: 14,925 closed and implemented, 157 closed but not implemented, and 567 open.

| Year | Recommendations | Reports |
|---|---|---|

- **Falling counts can mean different things.** Recommendations were mostly lower after 2015, for example 912 in 2016 and 602 in 2022. That could mean the problems got better. It could also mean OIG changed how it inspects, published fewer reports, or shifted its focus.

- **Some reports have no recommendations.** The report counts above include reports with no recommendations, because no other filters were applied.
- **OIG's open count differs.** OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations, while this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both. The difference is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

run.answer:
**No, these counts don't show growth.** Fewer reports had a recommendation mentioning suicide in 2025 than in 2024, but the drop mostly comes from a change in OIG's inspection programs, not clearly from less attention to suicide prevention.

The data is current as of **2026-11-04** (6 days old, not stale). Because these are totals across many reports, there's no single report to cite. The source is OIG's recommendations list: https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all

## The counts

| Year | Reports with a recommendation mentioning "suicide" | Matching recommendations | All reports with recommendations | Share of reports |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | **56** | 98 | 155 | ~36% |
| 2025 | **11** | 19 | 132 | ~8% |

Searching for "suicidal" gave exactly the same numbers. The search may treat the two words as the same, or they may simply appear in the same recommendations. I can't tell which.

## Why the number fell

Here are the matching recommendations broken down by type of report:

| Report type | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Comprehensive Healthcare Inspection Program (CHIP) | 55 | **0** |
| Hotline healthcare inspection | 18 | 2 |
| Vet Center inspection | 15 | 5 |
| National healthcare review | 8 | 3 |
| Mental health inspection program | 2 | **9** |

Almost all of the decline is in CHIP, which went from 55 matching recommendations to none. CHIP reports appear to have regularly included a review area that produced suicide-related recommendations. By 2025 there were no CHIP recommendations mentioning suicide, and none from its successor, the Healthcare Facility Inspection program. Meanwhile, matches in mental health inspection reports went up, from 2 to 9.

So there are two possible explanations, and the data supports both:
- **Things got better:** fewer facilities had problems related to suicide.
- **OIG changed how it looks:** the inspection rules changed, a different number of reports came out, or OIG shifted its focus. That would mean fewer chances to find these problems, not fewer problems. Since the drop lines up with the end of CHIP, this explanation looks strong. But I haven't checked what the new program reviews, so I can't confirm it.

## What the counts can show
- How many reports in each year had at least one recommendation using the word "suicide."
- Which types of reports those recommendations came from, and how that mix changed.
- A rough share of all reports with recommendations each year (56 of 155, then 11 of 132), which adjusts for how many reports came out.

## What the counts cannot show
- **Whether suicide prevention is growing as a theme.** The search only looks at the recommendation text, not the full reports. A report could discuss suicide prevention at length without its recommendations using the word "suicide."
- **What a recommendation is about.** Some suicide-prevention recommendations use other wording, like "safety plan," "lethal means," or "environmental risk." Those would be missed. A passing mention of suicide would still be counted.
- **Whether care improved.** Fewer recommendations doesn't mean better suicide-prevention practice at VA.
- **Whether facilities met their deadlines.** Target dates are the facility's own estimates. Closure dates seem to record when OIG reviewed the evidence and closed the item, which can be months after the work was done. A late closure, or an open item past its target date, doesn't show a facility missed its commitment.
- **How OIG labels these reports.** OIG has a "Suicide Prevention" topic tag, but it's applied to only about a quarter of reports, so I didn't count by it.

## Status, for context
- **2024:** all 98 matching recommendations are closed as implemented. Median time to close was about 232 days.
- **2025:** 6 of 19 are still open and 13 are closed as implemented. Three of the open ones, all from Vet Center reports, have been open more than a year. The oldest has been open 665 days.

One note on the data overall: OIG's dashboard lists 586 open recommendations, while this data has 567. A row-by-row comparison found the same recommendations in both. The difference is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

To get a better answer on the "theme" question, I could search for related wording ("safety plan," "lethal means," "suicide risk"), pull the reports OIG tagged "Suicide Prevention," or list the 11 reports from 2025 with their report numbers and links. Just tell me which you'd like.

**The median is 179 days, or about six months**, for Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA) recommendations. The data is current as of **2026-11-04** (6 days old, not stale).

**The numbers**
- **Median:** 179 days
- **Middle half of closures:** 134 to 312.5 days. A quarter closed within about 4½ months, and a quarter took more than about 10 months.
- **Sample:** 914 closed recommendations had dates that could be measured, out of 966 VBA recommendations in total (923 closed, 43 open).

**What it measures**
The number of days from when OIG published the report to when OIG marked the recommendation closed. Keep three things in mind:

1. **It's when OIG closed the item, not when VBA finished the work.** The closure date appears to record when OIG closed the recommendation after reviewing VBA's evidence, and that can come months after the work was done. So this measures the whole closure process, including OIG's review time, not just how fast VBA acted.
2. **It isn't a measure of whether target dates were met.** In the tool's words: *"A target date is the facility's own estimate... A closure after the target, or an open recommendation past it, does not show that a facility missed its commitment."*
3. **Some recommendations closed the day the report came out.** 110 were closed on publication day, presumably because they were fixed before the report was published. They're part of the 914, so they pull the median down somewhat.

**Notes from the data**
- 914 is smaller than the 923 closed items because about 6% of closed recommendations, mostly from 2013 to 2016, have no closure date on OIG's site.
- A recommendation assigned to two offices counts for both. Some VBA recommendations are shared with Information and Technology (11) or the Veterans Health Administration (5). Those are reported as separate groups, and the 179 days covers only the VBA group.
- No closure times were negative, so none were excluded.

**Open items and outcomes**
- **Open items:** 43 VBA recommendations are open. Their median age is 161 days, 17 have been open more than a year, and the oldest has been open 1,567 days (about 4.3 years).
- **Closed without being implemented:** 26 of the 923 closed recommendations (2.8%).

**Source:** VA OIG recommendations data, https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all. These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source.

**Data note:** OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations across all of VA, while this dataset has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both. The difference is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

Here are two examples of what facilities committed to do after OIG cited them for unsecured medication carts. Both recommendations are now **closed‑implemented**.

**1. Atlanta VA Medical Center, Decatur, Georgia: Report 13-03653-91** (published March 12, 2014)
Link: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-atlanta-va-1

- **What OIG recommended:** "processes be strengthened to ensure that medication carts are secured at all times and that compliance be monitored."
- **What the facility committed to:** Some carts didn't have working locks, so the facility said those carts were "being repaired and/or replaced." It had received six new carts, had 26 more on order, and was buying the rest. Until then, "medication carts are secured in a locked medication room unless in use." The BCMA Coordinator would also do "routine rounding in all inpatient areas to ensure and document compliance."
- **Status:** The target date was December 31, 2014, and the recommendation was closed March 11, 2015.

**2. San Francisco VA Health Care System, San Francisco, California: Report 15-00607-483** (published August 24, 2015)
Link: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-san-4

- **What OIG recommended:** "employees secure medication carts when not in use and that facility managers monitor compliance."
- **What the facility committed to:** The carts already locked themselves after a set time. The facility said staff had been told at every shift change that they must "physically lock carts and not to depend on the automatic time out." Charge Nurses and Nurse Managers would do random checks throughout the day, and the Unit Charge Nurse would do daily environment‑of‑care rounds. The daily Charge Nurse log would be reported at the monthly Nursing Division meeting and recorded in the minutes.
- **Status:** The target date was September 30, 2015, and the recommendation was closed April 7, 2016.

**What these show:** The first case was mainly an equipment problem. The facility fixed or replaced broken locks and kept carts in a locked room until the new ones arrived. The second was a staff habit problem: carts had working auto‑locks, but staff relied on them instead of locking the carts. That facility retrained staff and added several layers of checks.

**Notes:**
- The data is current as of **November 4, 2026** (6 days old, not stale).
- These two came from a ranked search, not a full count. The search tool says its shortlist "is not a count of findings," so it doesn't tell you how often OIG cites this problem. Other reports with similar commitments include Battle Creek (15-00606-495), West Palm Beach (15-00071-158), Palo Alto (13-00279-156) and Greater Los Angeles (16-00101-300).
- Both examples come from Combined Assessment Program reviews from 2014–2015, so commitments under OIG's current inspection program may look different.

# Preparing VA El Paso Healthcare System (Station 756, VISN 17) for its next OIG inspection

**Data as of 2026-11-04.** It's 6 days old and not stale. Everything below comes from OIG's public reports. It's not a rating of your facility, and it doesn't predict what OIG will find.

## 1. When the next inspection might happen (estimate only)
- **Estimated window: around January 2028.** OIG doesn't publish a schedule.
- **How the estimate is made:** Your last inspection end date plus about three years, since the program says it runs on a roughly three-year cycle. Counting from the publication date would give a later date, because reports usually come out months after the inspection.
- **Your last inspection:** Healthcare Facility Inspection, which ended 2025-01-16 and was published 2026-07-16. Report **25-00193-155**: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system

## 2. Your open recommendations (4 of 66 across 19 reports)
Inspectors will likely check on these first.

**From the 2026 Healthcare Facility Inspection (25-00193-155):**

| Rec | Finding | Target date | What your response committed to |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (Environment of Care) | "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment." | 2027-01-29 | Daily cleaning by Environmental Management Services (EMS), restroom cleaning logs and signs listing a contact number, an EMS tech checking high-traffic restrooms, 24 cleaning SOPs, EMS training finished June 2, 2026, daily oversight by the EMS Chief, and weekly Environment of Care rounds by the Associate Director |
| 2 (Primary Care) | "The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days." | 2026-12-31 | An SOP for secondary toxic exposure screening is being written, and results go to the Clinical Executive Council every month starting June 2026. The goal is zero screenings past 30 days for six months in a row |

**What to have ready:**
- **Rec 1:** Restroom logs, records showing staff completed the SOP training, and Environment of Care rounds data showing a trend over time.
- **Rec 2:** Finish and approve the SOP, then keep the monthly Clinical Executive Council reports. The six-month streak that began in June would end around November 2026, which is just before your Dec 31 target. A gap in any month would push it past that date.

**Other items in the same report that didn't get a formal recommendation.** These are worth checking again:
- Clean equipment stored in soiled utility rooms in the primary care and women's health clinics
- Expired respiratory masks in a locked clean storage room that Environment of Care rounds hadn't inspected in six months
- An emergency alert reset that was located inside the police station
- A damaged concrete floor in a women's restroom, which the VISN's FY2024 evaluation had also noted

Your response says the first three were fixed, but inspectors may check that the fixes held. The report notes the floor damage was a repeat of the VISN finding.

**From the 2023 Information Security Inspection (23-01179-204)**, https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare:
- **Rec 5:** "Ensure a video surveillance system is operational and monitored for the data center." (owner: OIT)
- **Rec 7:** "Ensure water detection sensors are implemented in the data center." (owner: OIT)

These have been open for over three years. No corrective action or target date was pulled from the report into this data. That doesn't mean nobody responded or that the items are overdue. It's still worth asking your local OIT what the current status is and what evidence they have.

## 3. Common findings at other facilities under the current program
Ranked by **how often they appear, not how serious they are** (out of 112 Healthcare Facility Inspection reports in scope):

1. **Workflows for communicating test results** (VHA Directive 1088(1)): 21 of 112 reports, 17 still open.
   - Example: Shreveport, **26-00057-170** (https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-shreveport-healthcare) wrote workflows for each service, set a training goal above 90%, and reports compliance to its Quality & Patient Safety Board.
2. **Test-result policy and monitoring whether patients were notified:** 12 of 112. The median time to close was 256 days (sample of 9).
   - Example: Hampton, **24-00603-86** (https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-hampton-healthcare-system) audits 50 outpatient results each month until it reaches 90% compliance for six months.
   - Example: Texas Valley Coastal Bend, **25-00189-199** (https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-texas-valley-coastal-bend) added service workflows as appendices to its local policy, plus an escalation sequence for lab staff reporting critical results.
3. **Clean environment to reduce infection risk** (VHA Directive 1608(1)): 11 of 112.
   - Example: Salisbury, **26-00030-213** (https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-salisbury-va-health-care) lets staff report cleanliness problems through its online request portal (LEAF), which notifies leadership.
   - Example: Central Arkansas, **25-00203-180** (https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-central-arkansas-veterans) has supervisors do monthly rounds, tracks findings until they're closed, and requires 90% compliance for three months.
4. **Stable leadership, with the VISN Director involved:** 9 of 112.
   - Example: Boston, **24-00613-162** (https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-boston-healthcare-system)
   - Example: Augusta, **24-00617-118** (https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-augusta-health-care-system)
5. **Keeping patient care areas clean and safe:** 9 of 112. The median time to close was about 192 days (sample of 10).
   - Example: St. Louis, **24-00600-136** (https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-st-louis-healthcare-system) audits 20 beds a month.
   - Example: Louisville, **24-03205-235** (https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-louisville-healthcare) does monthly inspections of dust under mattresses, requires 90% compliance for six months, and dusts sprinkler heads once a year.

**What this means for El Paso:** Items 3 and 5 overlap with your open Rec 1. The tool lists your facility as "not in" those groups only because your recommendation was filed under a different group (cluster 270). The peer audit methods above, with a fixed sample, a numerator and denominator, and a compliance goal over consecutive months, would give you measurable evidence for closing Rec 1. You haven't been cited for communicating test results, but it's the most common peer finding. Checking that each service has a written workflow that meets VHA Directive 1088(1) would be a good thing to do early.

## 4. Repeat findings
None were found for El Paso. **What counts as a repeat:** The same templated recommendation appearing in more than one of your reports. Only recommendations that were sorted into a group are compared. Because OIG uses a standard protocol, a repeat would only mean the issue was cited again, not that nothing was done in between.

## Notes on reading this data
- The peer findings are ranked by how often they appear, not how serious they are. They don't predict what OIG will find at your inspection. This server doesn't rate facilities.
- The peer examples are the closest matches by wording and meaning from other facilities, so not every one fits its group exactly. Target dates are each facility's own estimate, not a measure of missed deadlines.
- A group of findings points to a shared issue but doesn't prove a common cause, and one theme can be split across several groups. Read each median time to close together with its sample size. Recommendations closed on the day a report came out can pull a small group's median to 0 days. That's why the test-result workflow and clean-environment groups show medians of 0.
- If a finding has no facility response here, it just means none was pulled from the report. Responses come mostly from inspection reports.

If it helps, I can open the full 25-00193-155 report, pull more examples from other facilities for any of these themes, or look up how long Environment of Care recommendations usually take to close.

I can't give you that percentage. The public OIG record doesn't show whether target dates were met, and any figure I gave would be misleading.

**Why it can't be measured**
- **What a target date is:** The facility sets its own target date as an estimate.
- **What a closure date is:** It appears to be when OIG closed the recommendation after reviewing evidence. That review can come months after the work was finished.
- **What follows:** A recommendation closed after its target date, or still open past it, doesn't prove the facility missed its commitment. The gap may just be OIG's review time.

**What the data does show for VHA** (data as of 2026-11-04, 6 days old, so current)

| Measure | VHA |
|---|---|
| Recommendations | 13,440 |
| Closed, implemented | 12,978 |
| Closed, not implemented | 36 (a 0.28% not-implemented rate) |
| Open | 426 |
| Open more than 1 year | 108 |
| Median age of open items | 147 days (oldest: 2,078 days) |
| Median days from publication to closure | 225 (middle half: 153–326) |

**Notes on these numbers**
- **Shared recommendations:** A recommendation that names two offices counts for both. My VHA filter also pulled in some items VHA shares with other offices, such as OIT, OALC and EHRM IO.
- **Missing closure dates:** The days-to-closure figures cover 12,164 recommendations, not all 13,014 closed ones. About 6% of closed recommendations, mostly from 2013 to 2016, have no closure date on OIG's site. Another 11 had negative day counts and were left out.
- **Closed on publication day:** 946 VHA recommendations were closed the day their report came out, probably because they were fixed beforehand. That pulls the median down.
- **Open count:** Across the whole dataset, OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations and this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both; the gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source. They're based on OIG's recommendations listing (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all).

**Closer questions I can answer:**
- How many open VHA recommendations are more than a year old (108), and in which topics or report types
- How time to closure has changed by year
- For a specific report, each recommendation's target date next to its closure date and status history, without treating the gap as a missed commitment

**OIG doesn't name a "worst" VA medical center, and I can't build that ranking for you.** OIG reports document specific findings and recommendations at specific facilities. They don't score or rank medical centers, and the tools I use don't either.

Counting findings per facility wouldn't give a fair answer:
- **Inspection timing varies.** Facilities are inspected on different schedules and under different programs, so some have more reports simply because OIG has looked at them more often or more recently.
- **Report types differ.** A routine facility inspection, a hotline investigation of one complaint, and a national audit produce very different numbers of recommendations.
- **Size and complexity vary.** A large tertiary-care hospital with many services will usually have more findings than a small clinic.
- **More findings isn't the same as worse care.** The number of recommendations doesn't reliably reflect how serious the problems are or how quickly the facility fixed them.

**Here's what I can do instead, using OIG's public record:**
1. **Show one facility's record.** Give me a name, city or station number, and I'll pull its reports, recommendations, which are still open and any repeat findings, with report numbers and links.
2. **Find problems that recur across the VA**, such as medication safety, suicide risk screening or environment-of-care issues, and how many reports cite them.
3. **Look up serious findings by topic.** For example, I can search for patient-harm or quality-of-care findings, and filter by state, regional network (VISN), date or status.
4. **Measure how quickly recommendations get closed**, grouped by year, office, topic or report type, including how old the open ones are.

If you're thinking of a particular facility, or you're choosing where to get care, tell me which one or which area, and I'll pull its record.

**Nobody can tell you exactly, and I can't either.** OIG doesn't publish its findings ahead of time, and it doesn't publish an inspection schedule. What the public record can show is what El Paso was cited for before, what's still open, and what OIG often cites at similar facilities. That's useful for preparing, but it isn't a prediction.

The data is current as of **2026-11-04** (6 days old, not stale).

## When the next inspection might happen (an estimate only)
- **Estimated window: around January 16, 2028.**
- How that date was worked out: "The most recent inspection plus about three years, from the program's stated approximately three-year cycle. OIG does not publish a schedule. The count starts from the inspection's end date, or from the publication date where the report gives none… Publication usually comes months after the inspection, so an estimate from it tends to run later." Here the count starts from the end of the last inspection, January 16, 2025.
- That inspection's report: **25-00193-155**, published 2026-07-16. [Link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system)

## El Paso's own record (station 756, VISN 17)
There are 19 reports with 66 recommendations. **4 recommendations are still open.** These are the clearest things to have in order before the next visit:

| Report | Open recommendation | Facility's target date |
|---|---|---|
| [25-00193-155](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system) | "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment." | 2027-01-29 |
| [25-00193-155](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system) | "The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days." | 2026-12-31 |
| [23-01179-204](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare) | "Ensure a video surveillance system is operational and monitored for the data center." | none given |
| [23-01179-204](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare) | "Ensure water detection sensors are implemented in the data center." | none given |

The 2026 report also describes problems OIG found but didn't make recommendations about, because the facility had already fixed them by December 2025:
- Clean items were stored in soiled utility rooms.
- Expired respiratory masks were in a storage room that the environment of care team hadn't been able to get into.
- An emergency alert system at an outpatient clinic could only be reset from inside the locked police station.

The report also notes a damaged concrete floor in a women's restroom, which was a fall risk.

**Repeat findings:** none recorded. How repeats are counted: "The same templated recommendation in more than one report for this facility. OIG inspects against a standard protocol, so a repeat shows the same issue was cited again, not that nothing was done in between. Only recommendations in a cluster are compared."

## Findings OIG often makes at other facilities (current inspection program)
These are listed by how many reports they appear in, not by how serious they are.
1. **No written workflows for each team member's role in communicating test results** (VHA Directive 1088): 21 of 112 reports. Examples: [26-00057-170](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-shreveport-healthcare), [25-00254-277](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-william-s-middleton-memorial)
2. **Test-result communication policy or workflows not meeting VHA requirements, or no monitoring of whether patients are told their results:** 12 of 112. Examples: [24-00603-86](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-hampton-healthcare-system), [25-00189-199](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-texas-valley-coastal-bend)
3. **Keeping the environment clean to reduce infection risk** (VHA Directive 1608): 11 of 112. Examples: [26-00030-213](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-salisbury-va-health-care), [25-00203-180](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-central-arkansas-veterans)
4. **Stable, consistent facility leadership** (aimed at the VISN Director): 9 of 112. Examples: [24-00617-118](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-augusta-health-care-system), [24-00613-162](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-boston-healthcare-system)
5. **Keeping patient care areas clean and safe:** 9 of 112. Examples: [24-00600-136](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-st-louis-healthcare-system), [24-03205-235](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-louisville-healthcare)

El Paso's open finding about a clean and safe environment covers the same ground as items 3 and 5. That's worth noting, even though the data shows El Paso as not part of those groups (explained below).

## Limits on these numbers
- Peer findings are ranked by how often they appear, not by how serious they are, and they don't predict what an inspection will find. The data source doesn't rate facilities.
- The peer examples are the closest matches by wording and meaning from other facilities, and some may not truly belong to the listed group. Target dates are each facility's own estimate, not a measure of missed deadlines.
- When a facility is shown as not part of a group, that only means none of its recommendations were placed in that group. It doesn't mean the facility was never cited for that issue, because similar findings can sit in other groups.
- A group collects recommendations with matching wording or similar meaning. That suggests a shared issue but doesn't prove a common cause, and one issue can be split across several groups. Median closing times should be read together with the sample size: in a small group, recommendations closed the day the report came out can pull the median down to 0.
- When a finding shows no facility response, that only means none was pulled from the report. It doesn't show the facility failed to respond or that anything is overdue.
- OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations; this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both, and the difference is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

I can open any of these reports in full, or show in more detail what other facilities did to close a particular finding.
